title: Bad circumstances as the path
hookLine: third point: turn difficulties into practice

cards: The board flips from delayed to canceled. A groan goes down the gate area. Somebody is already shouting at the agent, who didn't cancel anything.
Your phone is at nine percent. The next flight is tomorrow. Two stories are available.
In one, the day is ruined, and the path, whatever you were practicing, is on hold until life calms down. In the other, this gate, this groan, this nine percent is the path.
Point three of the seven points of mind training picks the second story, on purpose.

teach.h: TURN EVERY MISHAP INTO THE PATH.
teach.b: First, the slogan that opens point three. In effect: when the world is full of trouble, turn every mishap into the path of awakening. Not after the trouble passes; through it.
A bad day isn't a break from practice. It's the material. Second, where the blame goes.
Another slogan says to drive all blame into one. That one isn't the agent, and it isn't you as a person to be beaten up.
In the commentaries it's self-cherishing, the me-first reflex that turns every delay into a personal insult. The trouble may be real; the commentaries trace the extra misery to that reflex.
Another slogan says to be grateful to everyone. The commentaries explain that a person who tests your patience gives you a chance to practice it that an easy person never could.

A story told about Atisha, which you met on day nine hundred sixty-nine, says he brought a difficult, short-tempered attendant with him to Tibet, and when asked why, called him his teacher of patience.

teach.h: NOT A TEACHING TO STAY IN HARM.
teach.b: It isn't a teaching to stay where you're being harmed, or to call injustice fine.

You can leave the gate, rebook, speak up; point three is about the mind that goes with you while you do. If someone is hurting you, you deserve safety: call local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.
And yesterday's tonglen fits here: breathe in the frustration of the whole gate, breathe out a little patience toward everyone stuck with you, including the agent.

how: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the slogans of point three in daily life, treating setbacks, illness and difficult people as occasions to practice patience, compassion and letting go of self-cherishing.

games.q: what does “bad circumstances as the path” mean?
o: using every mishap as the very material of practice
accepting harm quietly and never speaking up
waiting for trouble to pass before you practice

s: point three says to wait until life calms down to practice
it says to turn every mishap into the path, through the trouble, not after it.
drive all blame into one means beat yourself up
the commentaries point the blame at self-cherishing, not at you as a person.
a story says Atisha called a difficult attendant his teacher of patience
a story told about him; the point is that difficult people give patience a chance.

games.q: your flight is canceled. the gate area groans. someone is shouting at the agent. what does point three suggest?
o: treat this as the practice, and breathe patience toward everyone stuck.
pretend everything is fine and feel nothing.
games.why: point three turns mishaps into the path. you can still rebook and speak up; the practice is the mind you bring with you.

practice: Bring to mind a small annoyance from the last day or two, a splinter, not a big wound, and let it play once, noticing where the me-first reflex shows up: why me, how dare they.
Then try two moves from point three: point the blame at that reflex instead of at the person, and look for one thing the annoyance is teaching, patience, slowing down, anything.

wordCard.voice: Bad circumstances as the path. The third of the seven points: trouble isn't an interruption of practice; it's the practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan lam, path, the same lam as in lamrim, the stages of the path.

carryVoice: Your line: trouble is the path. Even at the gate, at nine percent. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: point three: transforming bad circumstances into the path (slogans on mishaps, blame and gratitude)
